newsitem.title: MEXICO: Sugar prices likely to stay in steady range - ISO.
newsitem.headline: Sugar prices likely to stay in steady range - ISO.

text.p: The head of the economic and statistics division of the International Sugar Organisation (ISO) said here Tuesday that the world sugar market is likely to see average raw prices in a range of 9.00 to 14.00 cents per lb.

Tony Hannah told the F.O. Licht World Sugar and Sweeteners' Conference here that the new structure of the international market would be the base behind the price stability, which markets have seen since 1987. He gave no time frame for his prediction.

"Several major shocks, such as Cuba's decline, Russia's consumption fall, Brazil's expansion, India's import of 1994, have occurred in the 1990s and the market has been robust enough for the price to remain in that range," Hannah told delegates.
"However, this does not mean that the price can never again exceed those levels. The Cuban decline alone, without balancing factors, could have done it," he added.
But he warned that because sugar had a price competitor in high fructoe corn syrup (HFCS), higher prices could damage the industry.
"Prices sustained above 15 cents/lb for two or three years could cause the kind of investment in HFCS that occurred in 1975-1985, resulting in a permanent loss of market for sugar," Hannah said.

HFCS use is widespead in developed nations such as the United States, where much of the soft drinks industry has converted to it use from traditional sugar-based sweeteners. Worries are that HFCS use will spread and expand in less developed nation, such as Mexico.

Historically, sugar has been one of the most volatile commodities. During a 1974 price boom prices hit 64 cents/lb, but they also fell below 8 cents/lb in 1978, rose back to 47 cents/lb in 1980 and dipped as low as 3 cents/lb in 1985.
Hannah pointed out that since 1987 prices have seldom been outside the range of 8.00 to 15.00 cents, and annual averages have moved in the range of 9.00 to 13.30.

"The reason for this transformation of the market is that high income developed countries have very low price elasticities, they are unresponsive to price change, while developing countries have high price elasticities. Consequently, with the current domination of the market by developing countries, if prices are less bought, and vice versa, so the price becomes more stable," Hannah said.
